title: HTTP vs HTTPS
summary: HTTP is the request-response protocol that powers the web. Learn about status codes, headers, methods, and how TLS handshakes enable secure HTTPS communication.

blocks.content: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a stateless client-server protocol. The client sends a request; the server returns a response.
HTTP methods express intent. GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (remove) form the basis of REST APIs. The URL + method combination describes what resource to act on.

items: Stateless: each request is independent — no previous state stored
Idempotent: GET/PUT/DELETE return the same result when repeated

blocks.content: HTTP status codes express the result of a request numerically. Ranges: 2xx (success), 3xx (redirection), 4xx (client error), 5xx (server error).
HTTP headers carry metadata for requests and responses: Content-Type (data format), Authorization (auth token), Cache-Control (caching policy), Accept-Encoding (compression).

items: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable

blocks.content: HTTPS adds TLS (Transport Layer Security) encryption to HTTP. It provides three guarantees: confidentiality (no eavesdropping), integrity (no tampering), and authentication (verifying the server).

The TLS handshake runs once on connection. The client and server negotiate a cipher suite, verify the server certificate, and securely exchange a session key. Subsequent communication uses fast symmetric encryption.

items: Certificate: CA (Certificate Authority) signs server's public key
Key exchange: ECDH → session key generation
HSTS: instructs browsers to only use HTTPS

blocks.content: HTTP/1.1 processes one request per connection, requiring multiple parallel connections for multiple resources. HTTP/2 uses multiplexing to handle many streams over one connection.
HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC (UDP-based). It eliminates TCP's head-of-line blocking and speeds up connection setup. Major sites and browsers now support HTTP/3.

items: HTTP/2: multiplexing, header compression (HPACK), server push
Enabling HTTP/2 on your server is the first performance step
